facts.text: In 1966 the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in the Philippines developed IR8 from a Taiwanese semi-dwarf variety, Dee-geo-woo-gen.
IR8 was nicknamed miracle rice and is credited with bringing the Green Revolution to tropical Asia.
IR8 is a semi-dwarf variety that resists lodging, that is, its plants do not easily fall over, and it responds well to nitrogen fertilizer.
Green Revolution varieties were short and lodging-resistant; this let farmers apply heavy nitrogen fertilizer, which raised grain yields.
Before 1950 farmers in tropical Asia mostly grew traditional varieties, and yields rarely went above about 2.5 tonnes per hectare.
In the 1966 dry season at IRRI's farm, IR8 yielded about 10.3 tonnes per hectare.
At experiment stations across tropical Asia, IR8 gave about 4 to 8 tonnes per hectare.
Irrigation and fertilizer were critical partners of the new high-yielding varieties.
The poorest areas, which relied on rain-fed farming, were the slowest to benefit from the Green Revolution.
Between 1960 and 2000, rice yields in all developing countries together rose by 109 percent, that is, they more than doubled.
Over about 50 years, cereal production in the developing world tripled while the cultivated land area grew by only about 30 percent.
Without improved crop varieties, about 20 to 25 million more hectares of farmland would have been needed worldwide.
Unintended effects included problems with water use, soil damage and chemical runoff.
Semi-dwarf varieties released after IR8 have about the same or lower yield potential than IR8, a yield plateau.
Pingali dates the first Green Revolution period to 1966 to 1985.
